{"id": "86:12/q05", "question": "What inward meaning is given to the earth's cleaving?", "turns_on": "Whether the inner earth is the body in relation to spirit or a condition of the heart and conduct.", "positions": [{"id": "86:12/q05/p1", "position": "The earth is the body, split when spirit departs at death or when spirit and body join.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī gives the two bodily moments; Bursevī repeats them and pairs the body's earth with the spirit's sky and its return in the second creation."}, {"id": "86:12/q05/p2", "position": "The heart turns back in remorse after sin.", "reasons": "Al-Tustarī distinguishes this inward reading from the outward emergence of vegetation."}, {"id": "86:12/q05/p3", "position": "The inward fissuring occurs through conformity in deeds and words.", "reasons": "Al-Tustarī gives this further inward account."}]}
{"id": "86:12/q06", "question": "Why are the returning sky and splitting earth paired?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize either generative complementarity, the analogy between growth and resurrection, or the contrast between changing oath signs and enduring speech.", "positions": [{"id": "86:12/q06/p1", "position": "Heaven acts from above and earth receives its effects, together producing life.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī shifts from animal to plant creation and likens sky and earth to father and mother. Biqāʿī likens upper and lower worlds to man and woman: heaven waters earth as a man waters a woman, and vegetation is like a child. Bursevī gives father, mother and child the same roles. Elmalılı says all three readings of earth's crack respond to effects from above; he reports the Sufi fathers-and-mothers analogy, relates rain and vegetation to reproductive fluid and seed with 86:6 and 36:36, and says this pair displays becoming and decay under God's creative, preserving power. Quṭb likens rain, growth, reproductive fluid and an embryo emerging from the womb."}, {"id": "86:12/q06/p2", "position": "Rain returning and plants emerging together make return after death intelligible.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī prefers this pairing and says it explains why rain is called al-rajʿ; he weakens other readings of al-rajʿ. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the vegetation reading fits rain as al-rajʿ, while Mujāhid's land-feature reading suits an alternate reading of al-rajʿ. Biqāʿī says the return of plants after decay parallels human return. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the paired oaths fit emergence from graves."}, {"id": "86:12/q06/p3", "position": "The changing sky and earth frame a sworn-to speech grounded in an unchanging reality.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the speech is fixed in the reality of its taʾwīl, which he promises to explain later."}]}
{"id": "86:12/q07", "question": "What does the earth's splitting show about resurrection?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "86:12/q07/p1", "position": "Life emerging from split earth shows God's power to restore people after death.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says new and renewed growth, including springs, points visibly to resurrection, and that restoring people is no different from restoring decayed plants. Bursevī calls plant emergence a sign as the earth opens. Al-Ālūsī prefers the rain-and-growth explanation because it foreshadows resurrection. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī relates the paired images to return to God and opening graves. Asad sees creative and re-creative power; Study Quran relates seasonal growth to humans emerging from base fluid in 86:6–8. Elmalılı includes graves opening for burial and rising. Al-Iṣlāḥī says the physical phenomenon makes the threatened Judgment certain and calls for preparation."}]}
{"id": "86:12/q08", "question": "What do these earthly and heavenly signs show about God?", "turns_on": "Whether the sign is described broadly as creative power and wisdom or through Quṭb's specific parallel with the star and exposed secrets.", "positions": [{"id": "86:12/q08/p1", "position": "They display God's creative power, wisdom and ordered making.", "reasons": "Asad says the returning sky and opening earth help one grasp creative and re-creative power. Elmalılı attributes life and its preservation to God and cites 36:36. Quṭb says the shared life and motion disclose a stable order and one maker unlike the things made. Kur'an Yolu sees divine wisdom in soft shoots piercing hard soil and treats the cosmic events as real manifestations of God's power. Bursevī says the repeated oaths display perfect knowledge and power."}, {"id": "86:12/q08/p2", "position": "The same divine craft joins the earth's splitting to the piercing star and the exposure of secrets.", "reasons": "Quṭb links the fissure with the piercing star of 86:3 and uncovered secrets of 86:9, inferring one maker from the repeated penetrating imagery."}]}
{"id": "86:12/q09", "question": "What is the rhetorical function of the oath by earth?", "turns_on": "Whether the note identifies the oath's structure, its assurance of Judgment and Qur'anic truth, or the abundance of benefits and divine attributes conveyed by repetition.", "positions": [{"id": "86:12/q09/p1", "position": "It is a second oath alongside the oath by heaven.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī identifies heaven as one oath and earth as a second; al-Māwardī says the earth readings he discusses are oaths. Al-Ṭabrisī says this further oath reinforces resurrection."}, {"id": "86:12/q09/p2", "position": "The cosmic oaths make the promised judgment and the Qur'an's truth emphatic.", "reasons": "Al-Iṣlāḥī says 86:11–14 use a physical phenomenon to establish that Judgment is certain, not jest. Quṭb says a categorical truth answers residual doubt, links the cosmic scene to the sūra's opening, and hears force and decisiveness in the expression's sound. Biqāʿī says the decisive signs and the Qur'an's eloquence make attack on it implausible. Kur'an Yolu says the signs are real and so is the Qur'an, which manifests God's speech."}, {"id": "86:12/q09/p3", "position": "Repeated oaths call attention to the signs' abundant benefits and God's knowledge and power.", "reasons": "Bursevī contrasts the first oath by sky with the later oaths by sky and earth and their descriptions."}]}
{"id": "86:12/q10", "question": "How does the mountain's splitting in 59:21 illuminate this image?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "86:12/q10/p1", "position": "It portrays lifeless rock as fearing God and becoming humble, using human inward responses as a rhetorical image.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes that fear and humility properly belong to the heart; her lexical discussion distinguishes cracking from shattering and mentions figurative rupture."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q01", "question": "What does sabbih command?", "turns_on": "Whether tasbih names declaration, a particular utterance, prayer, vocal praise, or a comprehensive devotional act.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q01/p1", "position": "Declare God free of all defects, false claims, rivals, and unworthy attributes and acts.", "reasons": "Muqatil makes this denial of shirk and affirmation of God's oneness. Zajjaj, Ibn Atiyya, Jishumi, Biqai, Ibn Ashur and others include evil, change, deficiency, idolatry, anthropomorphism, coercion, and claims of polytheists; Jishumi adds wisdom and goodness of divine acts. Elmalili includes spoken, inward, and practical worship; Qutb insists on inward awareness, not rote repetition. Ibn Ashur says the religious sense may be borrowed from Hebrew; Corpus Coranicum instead adduces Syriac shabbeh and the Hebrew psalmic imperative."}, {"id": "87:1/q01/p2", "position": "Say 'Glory be to my Lord, the Most High' as the command's verbal fulfillment.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Qatada and groups of Companions and Successors explain the command by the formula; transmitted recitation practice supports it. Alusi says an utterance of subhan requires treating ism as inserted. Tabari and Nahhas cite the Prophet's and Companions' practice in support of their interpretations."}, {"id": "87:1/q01/p3", "position": "Magnify and exalt the Lord.", "reasons": "Tabari reports that none is greater or higher. Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi say ism is added to magnify the referent; Labid's verse supports that idiom. Jarir's verse is cited for vocal devotional praise."}, {"id": "87:1/q01/p4", "position": "Pray to the Lord or pray using His name or command.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas variously says by the Lord's command or in His name, likening it to beginning in God's name with an omitted preposition. Mawardi adds mentioning Him at prayer's opening or holding Him in mind at intention; Razi cites prostration reports and 30:17. Elmalili notes prayer as a conventional tasbih sense but objects that the omitted preposition is against the surface construction; Alusi doubts the Ibn Abbas report."}, {"id": "87:1/q01/p5", "position": "Raise the voice in remembrance and praise of God.", "reasons": "Mawardi and Qurtubi cite Jarir's line about pilgrims chanting and magnifying God; Bursevi says this makes ism meaningful."}, {"id": "87:1/q01/p6", "position": "Practice sustained inward remembrance, obedience, and moral discipline.", "reasons": "Tustari joins outward denial of rivals to inward witnessing in prayer. Sulami forbids idle talk and lies afterward. Qushayri describes knowledge of the names and inward swimming in exaltedness; Islahi links remembrance and tahajjud to comfort, perseverance, protection from Satan, and a sound grasp of God. Qutb calls praise an experiential gift."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q02", "question": "What does ism mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the direct object is the divine word, an honorific stand-in for God, the act of naming, an attribute, or a broader sign.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q02/p1", "position": "God's name itself is the object of sanctification.", "reasons": "Tabari, Abu Hayyan, Alusi and Elmalili emphasize the direct object; the name must not be given to idols, misinterpreted, or used irreverently. Ibn Ashur says spoken reports and sacred attributes are applied to names designating God; purely inward conte

Alusi conditionally favors insertion if sabbih means utter subhan; Elmalili says sanctification of the referent still proceeds through its name."}, {"id": "87:1/q02/p3", "position": "Ism means naming, mention, or the act of speaking of God.", "reasons": "Tabari and others require fearful humility. Ibn Atiyya cites Arabic usage and the hadith on God's ninety-nine names for naming as an act. Qurtubi reports this but favors the named referent."}, {"id": "87:1/q02/p4", "position": "Ism means God's attribute or attributes.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim cites 7:180; Jishumi says to cleanse divine attributes of what is unfitting. Elmalili describes a Sufi account in which names are attributes and effects follow them."}, {"id": "87:1/q02/p5", "position": "Ism means God's oneness.", "reasons": "Damghani compares 73:8, taking glorification and remembrance of the name as affirmation of divine unity."}, {"id": "87:1/q02/p6", "position": "Ism means God's effects or created signs.", "reasons": "Isam al-Din says effects point to God as a name does and cites 67:3. Elmalili allows it as metaphor but finds leaving the ordinary linguistic sense remote."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q03", "question": "Do sabbih isma and sabbih bi-ismi mean the same thing?", "turns_on": "Whether bi- is freely alternating, semantically distinct, or understood as omitted in an interpretation of prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q03/p1", "position": "Both Arabic constructions convey the same glorification.", "reasons": "Al-Farra affirms both forms; Thalabi restricts the equivalence to contexts of remembrance and glorification. Razi reports the comparison with 56:74. Samarrai lists Quranic transitive and prepositional patterns."}, {"id": "87:1/q03/p2", "position": "The direct object sanctifies the name; bi- means glorifying God by means of His name.", "reasons": "Nahhas rejects a simple deletion of the preposition and says transitivity changes sense. Wahidi distinguishes the object from instrument; Elmalili says the chosen direct object deliberately sanctifies the name itself. Ibn Ashur says bi pairs speech with speech in other praise constructions."}, {"id": "87:1/q03/p3", "position": "An omitted bi- permits reading the command as praying in the Lord's name.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas compares 'begin in God's name'; Alusi doubts the transmission and Elmalili says the analysis opposes the apparent wording."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q04", "question": "Is God's name identical with the one named?", "turns_on": "Whether ism denotes a spoken designation or the divine referent, and whether the customary formula proves identity.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q04/p1", "position": "The name is identical with the named God in this context.", "reasons": "The author of al-Nazm says only God, not a distinct name, can be glorified. Baghowi and Qurtubi cite 'Glory to God/my Lord,' never 'Glory to God's name'; Sa'di al-Mufti uses the hadith formula likewise."}, {"id": "87:1/q04/p2", "position": "The wording and the entity differ; calling them identical equivocates or is tautological.", "reasons": "Razi says a word differs from its referent, while identity follows trivially if both terms denote the entity; perhaps confusion arose because 'name' is itself a noun for a timeless meaning. He rejects the formula argument since the verse admits several analyses. Alusi rejects identity."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q05", "question": "How must God's names be guarded?", "turns_on": "The scope of sanctifying a divine designation: assignment, interpretation, occasion and manner of speech, authorization, and figurative poetic address.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q05/p1", "position": "Do not transfer exclusive divine names to idols, false claimants, or creatures as God's equals.", "reasons": "Tabari cites al-Lat and al-Uzza; Nahhas derives the idol names from al-Aziz and Allah. Razi adds Musaylima's 'Merciful of Yamama.' Alusi distinguishes exclusive names from shared names used as equal providers. Tabatabai expands the rule to attributing divine acts to others and associating intercessors."}, {"id": "87:1/q05/p2", "position": "Interpret divine names without unworthy implications such as embodiment, spatial settlement, compulsion, or false likeness.", "reasons": "Kashshaf specifically opposes coercion and anthropomorphism. Baydawi and Alusi reject unjustified figurative interpretation as well as impossible literal senses; Ibn Ashur makes divine perfection the governing rule for ambiguous descriptions. Elmalili cites 42:11."}, {"id": "87:1/q05/p3", "position": "Utter God's names only with humility, understanding, and in fitting contexts.", "reasons": "Tabari and Thalabi stress reverent remembrance; Sulami warns against lies and idle talk afterward. Bursevi names yawning, relieving oneself, and excessive oaths. Alusi cites Malik declining to invoke God before a beggar who disliked hearing it. Ibn Ashur joins speech to understanding."}, {"id": "87:1/q05/p4", "position": "Avoid provoking unbelievers to insult God.", "reasons": "Tabari and Razi connect this to the prohibition on reviling pagan deities in 6:108."}, {"id": "87:1/q05/p5", "position": "Use only names established by revelation when naming God.", "reasons": "Razi cites 17:110 and the distinction from pagan whistling and clapping; Alusi's critics cite 7:180 against addressing God as Layla or Na'im. Bursevi reports the fixed-name position. Ibn Ashur says al-A'la is not separately counted among beautiful names because al-Ali already names the quality and names require name-like established usage."}, {"id": "87:1/q05/p6", "position": "Any designation free of deficiency may name God even if revelation did not establish it.", "reasons": "Razi attributes this to the Mu'tazilites, contrasting it with his revealed-name position."}, {"id": "87:1/q05/p7", "position": "Poetic Layla and Na'im are defensible as extended metaphors, without literally naming God by them.", "reasons": "Alusi reports a defense by allusion and analogy to allegorical readings of 2:67, says critics remain unsatisfied, and prefers a whole-expression metaphor; his full account compares metaphorical basmala interpretation."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q06", "question": "What does rabbika evoke?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q06/p1", "position": "The Lord is the creator, nurturer, benefactor, and governor; 'your' gives the Prophet a special personal address.", "reasons": "Biqai says the Lord formed and nurtured the Prophet in noble qualities; Qutb emphasizes tender care; Ibn Ashur says Rabb rather than Allah calls up creation and governance and the possessive honors the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q07", "question": "Who is commanded to glorify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q07/p1", "position": "The Prophet is directly addressed, with a charge that guides believers too.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur identifies the addressee; Biqai says the perfected Messenger understands how to glorify fully; Islahi reads the address as strengthening the Prophet amid his preaching fears."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q08", "question": "What does al-aʿla qualify?", "turns_on": "Case and the attachment of the following relative clause 'who created' in 87:2.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q08/p1", "position": "It qualifies rabb, 'Lord,' in the genitive.", "reasons": "Nahhas prefers this. Corpus Coranicum compares the Hebrew epithet following a divine title."}, {"id": "87:1/q08/p2", "position": "It qualifies ism, 'name,' in the accusative.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Tabrisi connect this to God's exalted names. {"id": "87:1/q09", "question": "What kind of highness does al-aʿla express?", "turns_on": "Whether highness denotes spatial direction, absolute excellence and power, ungraspable greatness, or a non-comparative adjective.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q09/p1", "position": "Supremacy in power, sovereignty, perfection, and rank, without spatial location.", "reasons": "Jishumi cites al-Farazdaq's poetry for honor and strength; Tabrisi compares al-akbar. {"id": "87:1/q10", "question": "Why is the Lord called al-aʿla here?", "turns_on": "The explanatory role of the epithet and the extent to which verse-end cadence explains its form.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q10/p1", "position": "His superlative rank makes transcendence fitting, and the following acts establish His power and care.", "reasons": "Biqai says rank is absolute. {"id": "87:1/q11", "question": "What variant wording or pronunciation is reported for this opening?", "turns_on": "Whether transmitted subhana phrases are variant text or recitation responses, and how the final vowel is pronounced.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q11/p1", "position": "The opening is recited as 'Subhana rabbiya al-aʿla,' sometimes followed by 'who created and proportioned.'", "reasons": "Ibn Umar, Ubayy, Ali, Abu Musa, Ibn al-Zubayr, Malik b. Dinar and others are named across sources. Reports vary between an actual alternate reading and a response after the canonical verse. Qurtubi denies the phrase is Quranic text; Corpus Coranicum retains the common imperative because similar imperatives open early Meccan passages."}, {"id": "87:1/q11/p2", "position": "The opening is also reported as 'Subhana ismi rabbika al-aʿla.'", "reasons": "Ibn Umar is heard using this form, attributed to Ubayy's reading; the reports vary in whether the possessive of subhana is ismi or rabbi."}, {"id": "87:1/q11/p3", "position": "A shorter wording, 'Sabbih rabbaka al-aʿla,' is reported.", "reasons": "Durr attributes this to Ibn al-Zubayr and al-Dahhak, who also directed the reciter to add the glorification."}, {"id": "87:1/q11/p4", "position": "The common imperative sabbih isma rabbika al-aʿla is retained.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum cites analogous early Meccan imperative openings, including 69:52 and 56:74; Qurtubi treats the added subhana phrase as devotional response rather than Quran."}, {"id": "87:1/q11/p5", "position": "The rhyme ending al-aʿla admits imala.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari says the imala of endings from al-a'la through Musa was treated in his earlier chapter."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q12", "question": "What should a reciter say after this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q12/p1", "position": "Say 'Subhana rabbiya al-aʿla' as a response to the command, including in prayer.", "reasons": "Reports name the Prophet, Ibn Abbas, Ali, Ibn Umar, Umar, Abu Musa, Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Dahhak, Qatada and al-Baqir. Abu Dawud notes Waki's raised Ibn Abbas report conflicts with mawquf versions from Abu Waki and Shu'ba. Itqan places the response within reflective recitation."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q13", "question": "What glorification belongs in prostration?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q13/p1", "position": "Use 'Subhana rabbiya al-aʿla' in prostration; the Great Lord's glorification belongs in bowing.", "reasons": "Reports from Uqba and others assign 87:1 to sujud after assigning 56:74, 56:96, or 69:52 to ruku. {"id": "87:1/q14", "question": "What occasion is reported for this verse's revelation?", "turns_on": "The reported triggering event: a human question about sujud or an angel's failed ascent and praise.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q14/p1", "position": "The Companions asked what to say in prostration; the verse descended and the Prophet supplied its glorification.", "reasons": "Abu Hurayra's version adds an odd number of repetitions; Durr and its full account also transmit the question."}, {"id": "87:1/q14/p2", "position": "An angel failed to reach the Throne despite multiplying wings, then glorified the Most High, prompting the verse and prostration instruction.", "reasons": "Qurtubi transmits the tale from Ja'far b. Muhammad through his forebears and gives no grading; the angel is called Hizqiyal in one account."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q15", "question": "Who first uttered this glorification?", "turns_on": "Which angel the distinct reports identify.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q15/p1", "position": "Michael was the first to say 'Subhana rabbiya al-aʿla.'", "reasons": "Ali's report and several later sources transmit this attribution; no grading is supplied in Qurtubi."}, {"id": "87:1/q15/p2", "position": "An angel named Hizqiyal said it after failing to reach the Throne.", "reasons": "Qurtubi's ungraded tale gives an extended story of multiplied wings and long flight before the utterance."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q16", "question": "Where and when was this sura revealed?", "turns_on": "Early transmission and thematic dating versus a later inference from possible references to Eid worship; chronology counts al-Fatiha differently.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q16/p1", "position": "The whole sura is Meccan, among the early revelations.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr and Aisha are reported; al-Bara says it was taught in Medina before the Prophet arrived. Ibn Atiyya calls the contrary Dahhak report weak; Alusi and Ibn Ashur say Eid and alms references do not prove Medinan origin. Ibn Ashur cites verse 6 and early themes."}, {"id": "87:1/q16/p2", "position": "The whole sura is Medinan.", "reasons": "Al-Dahhak is named; Ibn al-Faris connects the view to Eid prayer and end-of-Ramadan alms. Ibn Atiyya, Alusi and others dispute the inference on the strength of al-Bara's report and the lack of a decisive ritual reference."}, {"id": "87:1/q16/p3", "position": "Most is Meccan, but verses 14–15 are Medinan.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reports this from Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas in the full source."}, {"id": "87:1/q16/p4", "position": "It was seventh in the revelation order.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and al-Hasan place it in an early sequence after Iqra, Nun, al-Muzzammil, Tabbat and al-Takwir."}, {"id": "87:1/q16/p5", "position": "It was eighth, after al-Takwir and before al-Layl.", "reasons": "Jabir b. Zayd's count inserts al-Fatiha after al-Muddaththir; Ibn Ashur says either chronology is early and fits verse 6."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q17", "question": "What are the sura's names and verse count?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q17/p1", "position": "It is called al-Aʿla and also Sabbih or Subh, and has nineteen verses.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says al-A'la comes from a word unique to this sura and is favored by commentators and mushaf compilers, while the Prophet's Muadh report and Aisha's witr report use its opening; Baydawi and Ibn Kathir also call it Sabbih. {"id": "87:1/q21", "question": "How does the opening connect with the preceding sura and later verses?", "turns_on": "Different scopes of connection: the previous sura, the opening's foreshadowing, the whole sura's argument, and its historical setting.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q21/p1", "position": "It answers al-Tariq's themes of human creation, divine delay, and the seriousness of revelation with fuller praise of the Creator.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan links 86:5 and 86:13 to 87:1 and 87:6. Qutb adds afterlife recompense and the ease of message, messenger and community; Islahi sees gradual maturation of creation and human capacities."}, {"id": "87:1/q21/p4", "position": "The likely early setting of nearby praise and admonition is Mecca's Kaʿba cult.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum compares 73:2-5 and 74:2-3 and contrasts this with an already formed community's private devotions."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q22", "question": "Why does this sura open with an imperative of glorification?", "turns_on": "The formal series of praise openings, the pedagogic order of transcendence, and the sura's consoling purpose.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q22/p1", "position": "It completes a Quranic sequence of tasbih openings: verbal noun, past, present, and imperative.", "reasons": "The author of al-Ajaib and Biqai identify 17:1, 57:1, 59:1, 61:1, 62:1 and 64:1 as the earlier forms; Burhan describes fourteen praise openings and Abu Shama calls 87:1 both praise and command. Samarrai surveys verbal forms and object/preposition patterns."}, {"id": "87:1/q22/p2", "position": "The command starts with removing impossible notions before affirming attributes and teaching prophethood.", "reasons": "Biqai says clearing away defects precedes positive virtues, and theology proceeds through essence, attributes, self-subsistence and acts before prophethood; this counters imitation and denial and leads to obedience."}, {"id": "87:1/q22/p3", "position": "It grants the Prophet permission to praise God and prepares reassurance about revelation.", "reasons": "Qutb calls the permission itself a favor; Ibn Ashur says the imperative foreshadows verse 6 and fits the sura's purpose of steadying the recipient of revelation."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q23", "question": "Why are the following descriptions coordinated or separated in praise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q23/p1", "position": "Distinct attributes may be independently coordinated; varied syntax expands and strengthens praise.", "reasons": "Burhan says conjunction signals independent adjectives, citing Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa; separation is stronger when meanings differ widely. {"id": "87:1/q24", "question": "What theological claims are drawn from complete glorification?", "turns_on": "Razi contrasts sovereign ownership with Mu'tazilite moral goodness and human welfare.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q24/p1", "position": "God's essence and eternal attributes are free of composition and deficiency; His acts are those of the absolute owner.", "reasons": "Razi says God is neither substance nor accident, His attributes are not originated or finite, and no creature may object to His decisions. Duties bring God no benefit and rest on sovereignty."}, {"id": "87:1/q24/p2", "position": "All God's acts are good, and He neither does nor approves evil; duties serve people's interests.", "reasons": "Razi attributes these formulations to the Mu'tazilites, contrasting his ownership account."}, {"id": "87:1/q24/p3", "position": "God must be affirmed above both defect and wrongdoing, including false speech, futile creation, and neglect of reckoning.", "reasons": "Biqai applies the sura's transcendence to resurrection, justice, non-imitability of revelation and divine patience; Jishumi says God's acts are wise and good."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q25", "question": "How is the verse understood inwardly?", "turns_on": "Self-emptying through the Highest Name versus inward witnessing and remembrance.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q25/p1", "position": "The Highest Name encompasses God's essence and attributes; the soul's self-emptying lets divine perfections appear.", "reasons": "Qashani calls this the special praise of annihilation and says each thing glorifies through a particular divine name; Bursevi transmits this and adds each creature's own mode of praise."}, {"id": "87:1/q25/p2", "position": "Glorification joins outward denial of rivals to inward remembrance and witnessing only God.", "reasons": "Tustari locates this in prayer; Qushayri describes knowing the names, swimming inwardly in exaltedness, and intimacy that resists disobedience."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q26", "question": "What earlier language or scripture does this wording evoke?", "turns_on": "The proposed immediate language of influence, Hebrew or Syriac, and the biblical parallel.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q26/p1", "position": "Tasbih's religious praise sense may have entered Arabic from Hebrew.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur proposes Hebrew borrowing and connects it to 2:30."}, {"id": "87:1/q26/p2", "position": "The praise sense likely reflects Syriac shabbeh, itself translating Hebrew hillel and echoing psalmic hallelu-yah.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says Arabic 'swim/glide' cannot explain the devotional sense, compares Syriac prayer terminology, psalmic praise of God's name, and the epithet Hebrew elyon; the closest biblical construction is YHWH elyon."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q27", "question": "What broader devotional or human purpose does the opening serve?", "turns_on": "The spiritual effect of remembrance and the relation between voiced, enacted, and inward glorification.", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q27/p1", "position": "Recognition and remembrance of the Most High give people a patron, exemplar, path, courage, and perseverance.", "reasons": "Biqai says God, Muhammad and Islam meet these needs, citing the Prophet's confession, and that mercy enables obedience. Islahi says sound knowledge of God strengthens faith and conduct; remembrance comforts the heart in 13:28 and protects against Satan."}, {"id": "87:1/q27/p2", "position": "Praise of God's name is voiced publicly and privately, with fitting beliefs and acts, while inward thought glorifies God directly.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur links the direct object to spoken declaration, the name in 56:74, and timely action in 33:42; naming God One in 112:1 or 59:23 differs from arguing against idols without uttering a name in 22:73."}]}

{"id": "87:1/q29", "question": "What syntactic construction is elsewhere compared with 87:1?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q29/p1", "position": "A verb of glorification may substitute for a verb of remembrance while a prepositional phrase precedes the subject.", "reasons": "Burhan parses yusabbih as a substitute for yudhkar, with lahu fiha a fronted predicate and rijal the subject, citing 87:1 by analogy."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q30", "question": "What morphological pattern does al-aʿla illustrate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q30/p1", "position": "It is an afʿal form with the definite article.", "reasons": "Burhan lists three af'al patterns: construct, definite with al, and unmarked followed by min introducing the compared item, citing 63:8."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q31", "question": "How does sanctifying the name relate to knowing God's essence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q31/p1", "position": "Pure names express the essence's transcendence and are the human route to knowing it in this life.", "reasons": "Elmalili says minds know God through names, attributes or effects, while direct manifestation belongs to the afterlife; he relates this to 87:14-17."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q32", "question": "How should divine highness govern other attributes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q32/p1", "position": "Ambiguous descriptions must be interpreted in a way befitting the Most High's complete perfection.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur makes divine highness the standard for reading other attributes and requires figurative interpretation when literal description conflicts with it."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q33", "question": "What does God’s uniqueness mean for His attributes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q33/p1", "position": "God alone deserves His attributes and transcends the attributes of created things.", "reasons": "Jishumi presents this as a further explanation of the epithet."}]}
{"id": "87:1/q34", "question": "What did Ibn Umar say about speaking of God's name?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:1/q34/p1", "position": "He instructed not to say 'upon God's name,' since God's name is Most High.", "reasons": "Nafi transmits the remark; Qurtubi's full account repeats it."}]}
{"id": "87:2/q01", "question": "How does 'who created' attach grammatically to the preceding words?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause modifies Lord or name despite the intervening adjective and the problem of assigning creation to a name, or instead begins an implicit predication or praise.", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q01/p1", "position": "It qualifies 'Lord' or 'Most High' as another adjective.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says both adjectives can share one referent and compares the idiom yā Yazīd al-karīm dhū al-jumma. {"id": "87:2/q02", "question": "What does 'created' mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb describes origination, an initial form, or the assembly of parts before their proportioning.", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q02/p1", "position": "God brought things into existence from nonexistence.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says God can bring about whatever He wills without difficulty. {"id": "87:2/q03", "question": "Whom or what does God create and fashion, and in what way?", "turns_on": "The unstated object of 'created' may be every creature, living beings, humanity, Adam, or composed beings; the accounts also differ over whether fashioning concerns form, useful capacities, equal rulings, understanding, worship, or stages of gestation. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites the usual rule favoring a general omitted object; al-Ālūsī rejects unsupported restrictions.", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q03/p1", "position": "God creates all things and fashions them in sound, balanced, precise order without flaw.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī glosses taswiyah as adjustment; al-Naḥḥās adds that the results are good. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, and Abū Ḥayyān see harmony as evidence of a knowing, wise maker; Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says it displays power and oneness. Al-Rāzī attributes the order to God's knowledge and power. Al-Ālūsī says each essence and attribute is formed as wisdom requires, rejects narrower objects as unsupported, and notes that the omitted object gives general scope. Al-Qurṭubī recalls his explanation at 82:7; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites precise fingertips and 91:7 and 75:38. Q 67:3–4 is cited by Study Quran for the absence of flaw. Ibn Kathīr calls each creature's form the finest."}, {"id": "87:2/q03/p4", "position": "God creates living beings and proportions their limbs and senses.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī names hands, feet or legs, and eyes; al-Rāzī adds each animal's needed organs, tools and senses. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports al-Zajjāj's human object, while al-Ālūsī says this restriction lacks textual support."}, {"id": "87:2/q03/p6", "position": "God brings humans into being and then perfects their form.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī transmits this as one possibility. {"id": "87:2/q04", "question": "What is the sense of 'fashioned' (sawwā) as a word?", "turns_on": "The word's range includes equality, adjustment, straightening, improvement, and perfection; Iṣlāḥī says the context selects perfection.", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q04/p1", "position": "It means making proportionate, adjusted, straight, or precise.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī calls it adjustment; Jishumī says equality in form, rank, status, or any respect. Al-Ālūsī calls proportion its original sense; Ibn ʿĀshūr glosses it as straightening and precise making, citing 91:7 and 75:38. Iṣlāḥī also notes senses of improving and flattening, while choosing perfection here."}, {"id": "87:2/q04/p2", "position": "In this context it means completing or perfecting what is made.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī contrasts possible senses of improving or flattening and says context selects perfecting; he also pairs an initial sketch with its later completion. {"id": "87:2/q05", "question": "What does the 'fa' between creating and fashioning express?", "turns_on": "Whether the ordered verbs mark a conceptual and causal sequence accompanying one act, or emphasize observable stages of human development.", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q05/p1", "position": "It makes fashioning the consequence and chief point of creation, ordered in thought though simultaneous in occurrence.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares Ibn Ziyāba's poem, where a raid, plunder, and escape provide the ordered groundwork for grief; creation likewise precedes fashioning in the observer's understanding. Al-Biqāʿī says creation requires proportion for balance."}, {"id": "87:2/q05/p2", "position": "The sequence reflects a gradual development from initial making to completed form.", "reasons": "Muqātil describes drop, clot, and morsel of flesh in the womb before proportionate formation; Iṣlāḥī says God's works unfold gradually in wisdom, and a human sketch passes through stages before completion."}]}
{"id": "87:2/q06", "question": "Do the perfect verbs describe only past creation or continuing activity?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q06/p1", "position": "Their perfect form is aspectual; creation continues as ongoing world-sustaining activity.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum points to pasture's recurring growth and decay in 87:4–5 and compares 53:43–49, 96:1–5, and 95:4–5."}]}
{"id": "87:2/q07", "question": "What divine claim does the clause make about human acts?", "turns_on": "Whether universal creation includes human acts without qualification, or allows mediated creation by God's granting human capacities.", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q07/p1", "position": "God's universal creation includes human acts and challenges the claim that humans create their own acts.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī appeals to the verse's unrestricted generality against the Muʿtazilī claim."}, {"id": "87:2/q07/p2", "position": "God creates human acts directly or through enabling people and granting their capacities.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī suggests this as a possible way to understand al-Zamakhsharī's broad wording despite his Muʿtazilī commitments; he also allows that al-Zamakhsharī may avoid strict universality."}]}
{"id": "87:2/q08", "question": "How does creating relate God to creatures?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q08/p1", "position": "As Creator, God is above created beings and free from their contingency, beginning, and need for a cause.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says creator and creature must not be confused in names or attributes, and the Lord is superior to those He nurtures."}]}
{"id": "87:2/q09", "question": "How does this creation clause bear on God's exaltedness?", "turns_on": "How the surrounding acts establish divine worthiness of praise and what the superlative language does or does not imply.", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q09/p1", "position": "It shows exalted power and lordship through creation and proportioning, in a way befitting God's majesty.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī rejects a spatial reading because distance does not establish worthiness of praise, while these acts display power. Al-Qurṭubī's teacher says the clauses explain God's exaltedness above creatures."}, {"id": "87:2/q09/p2", "position": "The descriptions 'Great' and 'Highest' do not imply multiple gods or a comparison with another lord.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī rejects that objection because God's oneness is already established and no other lord is mentioned."}]}
{"id": "87:2/q10", "question": "What inward significance is given to creation and fashioning?", "turns_on": "Whether fashioning's spiritual consequence is distinctive guidance, readiness for the perfect spirit, or receptivity to an allotted effusion.", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q10/p1", "position": "Humans receive a special gift of guidance; pride belongs in guidance and piety rather than created form.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī cites 49:13; Bursawī reports a related view that creatures share basic creation but differ through special guidance."}, {"id": "87:2/q10/p2", "position": "The outward human constitution is proportioned to receive the most complete spirit and every perfection.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī speaks of a particular temperament; Bursawī transmits the same reading as the body receiving the perfect spirit."}, {"id": "87:2/q10/p3", "position": "Each being is formed to receive its allotted divine effusion according to innate capacity.", "reasons": "Bursawī attributes this interpretation to the Najmiyya."}]}
{"id": "87:2/q11", "question": "How do creation and fashioning support the command to glorify God?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause's immediate lesson is the observable proof warranting glorification or the gradual divine ordering that calls for patience.", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q11/p1", "position": "They answer why the Lord is known and worthy of glorification by displaying observable divine power, wisdom, and guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī calls creation and guidance a central prophetic proof: Abraham says his Creator guides him (26:78), Moses describes the giver of each thing's form and guidance (20:49–50), and the opening revelation joins creation and teaching (96:1–4). He says their abundant marvels are directly observable. Jishumī says the sūra answers the preceding warning with God's attributes and power. Al-Biqāʿī and Ibn al-Zubayr connect the preceding servants' or unbelievers' plots with the command to glorify and the demonstration of power and wisdom. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the first four verses prove absolute lordship; Ibn ʿĀshūr says they indicate oneness through human creation and sustenance."}, {"id": "87:2/q11/p2", "position": "The ordered acts explain the gradual maturing of created physical and intellectual capacities and counsel patient obedience.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says verses 1–5 address the Prophet's preaching fears; divine plans unfold by wisdom, so delays are wise and hardship can benefit people in both lives."}]}
{"id": "87:2/q12", "question": "How does this clause relate to neighboring sūras and later verses of this sūra?", "turns_on": "The notes trace different links: the preceding sūra's warning and resurrection argument, the Prophet's later promises in this sūra, and the sūra's broader themes.", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q12/p1", "position": "It carries al-Ṭāriq's account of human origin toward proof of resurrection and exposed secrets.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī cites 86:5 and 86:8–9; Ibn al-Zubayr also ties the plot at 86:15 to the command at 87:1 and creation and guidance at 87:2–3 as evidence against slander. Iṣlāḥī says the prior sūra warned persistent deniers that their respite is temporary and that this sūra turns chiefly to the Prophet's fears."}, {"id": "87:2/q12/p2", "position": "God's fashioning and guidance anticipate the Prophet's capacity to retain revelation and receive an easy law.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 87:6 and 87:8 and says God equipped the Prophet for the burdens of mission; Iṣlāḥī describes a sequence of sūras dispelling his preaching fears."}, {"id": "87:2/q12/p3", "position": "This creation account belongs to a sūra praising the Creator's oneness alongside revelation and afterlife recompense.", "reasons": "Qutb says the sūra makes the cosmos a sanctuary of praise, reassures the Prophet with divine preservation and ease, and roots its themes in earlier scriptures (87:18–19). Ibn ʿĀshūr says 'Most High' honors the Quran and steadies its reception as God's speech."}]}
{"id": "87:2/q13", "question": "Which other passages or expressions parallel the pairing of creating and fashioning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q13/p1", "position": "The two verbs also occur together at 82:7 and 75:38.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum names both parallels; Ibn al-Jawzī refers readers to his explanation at 82:7. Ibn ʿĀshūr also invokes 75:38 when explaining precise fashioning."}, {"id": "87:2/q13/p2", "position": "Creation and determination express the specification that precedes and accompanies particular existence.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī groups 87:2–3 with 15:21, 54:49, 25:2, 57:22 and 64:11, saying things descend from undetermined plenitude into particular existence with determined relations to other existents."}]}
